lesson_title: Zero Is the Only Number That Talks
hook_text: Two friends' takings multiply to zero. You instantly know something. Multiply to R800 — you know nothing. That's the whole rule.
clip_script: Two friends run a stall for a day. You're told their takings, multiplied together, come to zero. What do you know? Instantly: at least one of them sold nothing. There's no other way to get zero out of a multiplication. Now change it. Their takings multiply to eight hundred rand. What do you know about the first one? Nothing. Could be eight hundred and one. Could be forty and twenty. Could be four and two hundred. Every split works. THAT is why your teacher screams 'make it equal zero' before you factorise. Zero is the only number that forces a confession out of a product. So when you see x minus two, times x plus five, equals eight — you may NOT say x minus two is eight. Expand it. Subtract the eight. Get x squared plus three x minus eighteen equals zero. Now factorise: x plus six, times x minus three. Now one bracket has to be empty. Minus six, or three. And one more thing that costs a mark every year: never divide an equation by x. That's removing a suspect from the line-up before anyone gets questioned.
visual_style: A township stall at closing time: two cash tins, one snapping empty as a zero flashes; then coins scattering into many possible splits when the total is R800; brackets closing around a line of algebra like tin lids.
pacing: Snappy setup, hard stop on the word 'nothing', brisk run through the worked line.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and stop losing marks on the easiest quadratics in the paper.
